articles.title: Bottlenose whales may look after each other when they’re sick
articles.summary: Northern bottlenose whales are more likely to stick together when individuals are poorly or emaciated
articles.content:
Northern bottlenose whales are more likely to stick together when individuals are poorly or emaciated

Bottlenose whales have more companions when they are sickly than when they are seemingly healthy Flip Nicklin/Minden Pictures/Alamy

Northern bottlenose whales have stronger social bonds when they are starving or sick. This discovery was a surprise, because often in mammals, social connections are associated with better health. But during tough times, these whales may rally round and care for others in need.

That idea fits with early whalers’ descriptions of the animals’ behaviour. In a report from 1882, David Gray, commander of the whaling steamer Eclipse, said he had observed thousands of northern bottlenose whales, and noted they had a peculiar response to injured individuals. “The herd never leaves a wounded companion so long as it is alive,” he said. “They come from every point of the compass towards the struck one in the most mysterious manner.”

But such observations are hard to make. Northern bottlenose whales (Hyperoodon ampullatus), which belong to a relatively mysterious whale family known as beaked whales, live in isolated parts of the ocean and spend most of their time diving deep for food. “Seeing and studying this elusive species is not easy at all,” says Olaf Meynecke at Griffith University in Brisbane, who wasn’t involved in the research.

Advertisement

But Hal Whitehead at Dalhousie University in Halifax, Canada, and his colleagues have been studying a local group of northern bottlenose whales since the 1980s. This population is centred over a deep submarine canyon, a day and a half sail from Halifax.

The team has collected a database of photographs, taken as the animals come to the surface, stretching back 37 years. Different whales can be identified in the pictures from markings on their fins, providing a rare opportunity to track their lives over decades, says team member Sam Walmsley at Princeton University.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter

The researchers recorded whether the whales looked plump or emaciated, as a marker for health. Around 11 per cent of the whales were classified as being in poor condition at any particular time. To map their social relationships, the researchers recorded which companions the whales appeared with in the photographs.

Walmsley expected to see a positive correlation between social bonds and health, as has been reported in many mammals, from mice to baboons. “If a whale is in poor condition, maybe it just needs to focus on getting enough squid [or] enough fish to survive,” he says, rather than investing energy in socialising. But, in fact, the sickly whales had more social partners than was normal for this species, and they hung out in larger groups.

The reasons for this are unclear. Maybe sick whales are more likely to seek out others, says Walmsley, or maybe whales that are already in bigger groups have to compete more for food. But an interesting possibility, he says, is that “the whales are attracted to these whales in poor condition, maybe providing some additional support”.

Caregiving would fit with what is seen or suspected in other cetaceans, too, says Meynecke, even if it can be hard to prove. Humpback whales, which Meynecke studies, aren’t particularly sociable, but they share information about food abundance and hunt together if times are hard, he says. “We are seeing that when they are stressed, they do assist each other.”

For Walmsley, the finding also helps to put human relationships into context, as evidence mounts for how damaging social isolation can be for our health. “I think getting more specific about how health and sociality are related in a wide range of mammals is part of what helps us to think about the evolutionary side of that,” he says.

This positive, substantive finding has broad significance beyond a niche audience.
articles.personality_title: Northern bottlenose whales show care by staying close when sick
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Northern bottlenose whales are a type of deep-diving whale that live in isolated ocean areas. They are hard to study because they spend most of their time underwater and far from shore. Scientists have been watching a group of these whales near Canada for decades, using photos to identify individuals and learn about their lives.

**What happened** – Researchers found that when these whales are sick or very thin, they tend to stay in larger groups and have more companions than when they are healthy. This was surprising because in many animals, being sick usually means less social contact. The study used 37 years of photographs to compare the whales’ health and social behavior.

**Impact** – This discovery suggests that northern bottlenose whales may care for each other during hard times by sticking together. It matches old reports from whalers who saw whales staying close to injured companions. This kind of behavior shows that some whales might support each other when they are weak, which adds new understanding to how animals live and survive together.

**What’s next step** – Scientists want to learn why sick whales gather more—whether they seek help, or if healthy whales support the sick. They also hope to study if this kind of care happens in other whale species. Understanding these social bonds could help explain how health and friendships connect in animals, including humans.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Northern bottlenose whales form stronger social groups when sick, showing possible care and support within their community.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les baleines à bec nordiques restent proches quand elles sont malades
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les baleines à bec nordiques sont un type de baleines qui plongent profondément et vivent dans des zones isolées de l’océan. Elles sont difficiles à étudier car elles passent beaucoup de temps sous l’eau, loin des côtes. Des chercheurs observent un groupe de ces baleines près du Canada depuis des décennies grâce à des photos qui permettent d’identifier chaque individu.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les chercheurs ont découvert que lorsque ces baleines sont malades ou très maigres, elles restent dans des groupes plus grands et ont plus de compagnons que lorsqu’elles sont en bonne santé. C’était une surprise, car chez beaucoup d’animaux, les malades sont souvent moins sociaux. L’étude a utilisé 37 ans de photos pour comparer la santé des baleines et leur comportement social.

**Impact** – Cette découverte suggère que les baleines à bec nordiques pourraient s’entraider en restant proches quand elles traversent des moments difficiles. Cela correspond à de vieux récits de chasseurs qui avaient vu des baleines rester près de compagnons blessés. Ce comportement montre que certaines baleines pourraient soutenir les autres quand elles sont faibles, ce qui enrichit notre compréhension de leur vie sociale.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent comprendre pourquoi les baleines malades se rassemblent ainsi : cherchent-elles de l’aide, ou reçoivent-elles du soutien des autres ? Ils espèrent aussi étudier si ce comportement existe chez d’autres espèces de baleines. Mieux comprendre ces liens sociaux pourrait expliquer la relation entre santé et amitiés chez les animaux, y compris les humains.

**Phrase clé** – Les baleines à bec nordiques forment des groupes plus forts quand elles sont malades, montrant un possible comportement de soin et de soutien.
articles.personality_title_es: Las ballenas de pico norteñas se acercan cuando están enfermas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las ballenas de pico norteñas son un tipo de ballenas que bucean muy profundo y viven en zonas aisladas del océano. Son difíciles de estudiar porque pasan mucho tiempo bajo el agua y lejos de la costa. Científicos han estado observando un grupo de estas ballenas cerca de Canadá durante décadas, usando fotos para identificar a cada una.

**Qué pasó** – Los investigadores descubrieron que cuando estas ballenas están enfermas o muy delgadas, tienden a agruparse en grupos más grandes y tener más compañeros que cuando están saludables. Esto fue una sorpresa porque en muchos animales, cuando están enfermos suelen estar menos sociales. El estudio usó 37 años de fotos para comparar la salud y el comportamiento social de las ballenas.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo sugiere que las ballenas de pico norteñas podrían cuidarse unas a otras quedándose cerca cuando pasan momentos difíciles. Esto coincide con antiguos relatos de balleneros que vieron a las ballenas quedarse junto a compañeros heridos. Este tipo de comportamiento muestra que algunas ballenas pueden apoyarse cuando están débiles, lo que ayuda a entender mejor cómo viven y sobreviven juntas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren saber por qué las ballenas enfermas se juntan más: si buscan ayuda o si las ballenas saludables les dan apoyo. También esperan estudiar si este cuidado ocurre en otras especies de ballenas. Entender estos lazos sociales puede ayudar a explicar cómo la salud y la amistad están conectadas en animales, incluidos los humanos.

**Frase clave** – Las ballenas de pico norteñas forman grupos más fuertes cuando están enfermas, mostrando posible cuidado y apoyo dentro de su comunidad.

articles.title: Why failure is a taboo topic in science
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03328-0Failure is one of the best teachers we have. So why is nobody talking about it?
articles.content:
Stephen Webster 00:04

But I just want to welcome you, those of you who are external to Imperial.

Of course, those of you who are at Imperial, welcome too.

It’s not often we can get together as colleagues to discuss these kinds of things.

That’s me kicking off the opening session of the Failure in Science conference.

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture and what we don’t.

And of course, being a university, that means conferences.

And this one, Failure in Science, has really got a lot to do with Magdalena Skipper sitting here because she said to me this time last year, ”Should we have a conference on failure in science?”

And I just thought, Imperial College, Nature magazine, a conference about failure. You know, this is really too good to be true. Let’s work on this.

So, and so Magdalena Skipper, (she’s editor-in-chief of the journal Nature), and I got to work.

And in April 2026 at Imperial, we welcomed 150 delegates, all of them eager to talk about something not much talked about: failure in science.

We spent the day focused on stuff going wrong, mistakes being made, opportunities being missed, and good things just being neglected.

In this series of six podcasts, using the conference as a springboard, we’re exploring different aspects of failure.

That means much more than simply looking at failure as something personal, a spot of bad luck coming our way.

When it comes to science, is there institutional failure too? For example, should universities frame failure not as a problem, but as part of a creative process, as part of good science? How can institutions look more sympathetically at failure and see failure as a necessity when quick progress is so often the bottom line.

And we’ll also look at the impact of science more widely. What can go wrong when scientific knowledge leaves the lab and tries to make a difference in society?

But first, in episode one, over to Magdalena Skipper.

Magdalena Skipper 02:41

First of all, actually, I want to start by thanking you and Imperial for following up on what I honestly did not think you were going to follow up on.

Because failure is a taboo topic.

Even though we know that failure is part of success, failure is one of the best teachers that we have, as long as we learn from those failures and don’t repeat those mistakes.

I’m Magdalena Skipper. I am editor-in-chief of Nature.

At the conference, I talked about the fact that failure is often a taboo. We don’t talk about it. We know that in science, failure is an everyday occurrence, and of course, failure itself is a very large umbrella term.

Most experiments fail. We learn from that failure, a great deal. Sometimes our plans in our career fail. We learn from that as well. We have to back up and pivot in another direction.

Considering how useful those lessons are, how contextualized they are, I find it surprising that we don’t talk more about failure, that we’re not more honest about the role that failure plays.

But we are petrified of it.

If you failed, you’re a loser, and that’s why nobody wants to talk about it.

Hence, it’s a taboo.

Failure is part and parcel of our lives, be it professional or personal. We learn through failure. There isn’t a single individual who hasn’t failed at something.

The really crucial aspect of it is how much we learn from it. We learn it’s a matter of building resilience, but it’s a matter also of delving deep into the topic, into the situation in which we have failed, and understanding it much, much more deeply in a much more nuanced way.

So, on the one hand, it’s a natural process. There isn’t a person or a system that hasn’t failed at some point. And on the other hand, it’s such a useful teacher.

The conference was part of a wider project called the Good Science Project, and in the end, the day focused on a number of levels.

One was an individual level. How individuals fail themselves and how they feel about it, how they recover from it, what they learn from it.

We talked about what failing means at an institutional level, or an organizational level.

And of course, since science or research more broadly doesn’t just happen in an academic setting, we also talk about how failure is dealt with in other settings, in the private sector, in in society more broadly.

Much later on in my professional career, I made a decision to step away from scientific, active scientific research and become a scientific editor.

I did that after a PhD and after a postdoc. And now, for me, looking back over the years, I think that was, without a doubt, the best professional decision I ever made. But to some who are wedded to the idea that the only true path for a researcher is to continue in active research, that was a sign of my failure.

I failed to be a successful academic researcher.

And it’s really interesting because that one act, that one action that I took, for me, was a manifestation of success or successful decision, and a manifestation of failure for others.

So I have been referred to as a failed scientist. And of course I’m a failed many other things.

Once upon a time, I wanted to be a firefighter. I’m also a failed firefighter. That never came to pass.

I think the most important thing is that I don’t fail all the time at what I’m actually doing right now.

And perhaps the next thing to add is, in general, in failure, if you do fail, learning from that experience so you move on, and you move on as a richer individual, a richer professional, is really important.

Think about the following example...

If you are constantly petrified of failing, you are going to play safe all the time. You’re not going to take risks. You’re not going to place big bets, if you like.

Now, in science, that translates into addressing big questions, formulating risky hypotheses, deciding to dedicate funding to a risky, perhaps long-term project that is not fail-safe, is not something that, broadly speaking, we already understand, and you colouring in the boxes or filling in the blanks.

No, if you are not afraid of failure, you are more likely to take bigger risks. And of course, when you take bigger risks, yes, there is a risk of failure.

But there is a risk of there’s a possibility of of great of great gain. Now, our general aversion towards failure means that in our funding systems, we tend to we tend to prefer to fund projects that have quite a lot of foundation, that is safe already.

Many scientists have the experience when they apply for grants, that a large proportion of what it is they’re proposing in the grant they already know is going to work because they have demonstrated it at some smaller level to a smaller degree.

So the question then becomes: is our funding system really designed to push the boundaries of knowledge and make us take those risks and discover something completely unknown, take us in a new direction, maybe open a new avenue, maybe even create a new discipline, or uncover a new approach to probing some questions?

Or is it more designed to walk, take very small steps in some direction?

It’s fascinating to consider the different attitudes that different sectors, different industries have towards failure.

But my understanding is it’s a practice that is relatively widespread in technology companies, especially in Silicon Valley.

And the practice is as follows. In order not to stifle and prevent that risk-taking attitude, which may lead to failure, those companies actually reward their employees financially for failing.

But if they fail fast, imagine without this incentive, you have a situation where only the employees-and this is in the research setting within Google X, only the employees that come up with quote unquote ”positive results”, something that can be taken forward, are rewarded.

But those positive results may be less impactful, or less influential, or have fewer implications if all the employees are thinking: Oh, I will only get rewarded if I succeed. I therefore must not fail at all cost.

That really influences your risk taking.

Now, of course, from a company’s perspective, there’s no point investing employees’ time or money in long-term pursuit of a project that fails. So what is being rewarded is fast failure. That is crucial.

That is failing fast. To me, it’s a really interesting way of incentivizing risk-taking.

Basically, ultimately, of course, everyone wants to succeed, but the road to that success often leads through failure, and maybe there isn’t another way. Maybe you have to go through failure in order to get to that success.

And contrasting that to an academic setting, where often a lot of time and money is invested in long-term projects, then there should have been a stop, no go decision made earlier on, but perhaps I’m sure there are a number of reasons why a similar approach is not adopted in academic setting.

But one of them I would suggest is that fear of failure? Once you have a project, it’s your project, it’s your baby. You’ve created it. You need to continue proceeding with it.

At the conference I mentioned one specific example of how failure can really energize and motivate researchers.

So the specific example, it’s an example of a paper, a scientific paper, describes a metascience study, so a science of science, where the researchers obtain data from a funder, a US funder, looking at a population of scientists around the cutoff bar for funding.

So they looked at a small, small sliver of this population just above that cutoff. So individuals who just scraped in and got the funding. And then those individuals who just didn’t make it, who just didn’t get the funding. They followed those researchers through time.

And the really interesting finding is that those who just failed to get the funding did better in terms of their career, establishing their career, and contribution to science, than those who just got the funding.

Now that was an observation in the paper. We can speculate why there might be, but I myself find it particularly compelling to think that it’s almost a demonstration of a saying: What doesn’t kill you make you makes you stronger.

That if you’re really convinced that you have a great idea, that you are committed to pursuing a scientific career, and you failed in gaining this support, financial support, then you will find another way.

And that induces that inventiveness and creates a greater motivation for you to persevere, because you are sure that you need to succeed.

So here, failure gives you a boost, if you like, is an additional motivator.

We all know, we have discussed already, that science progresses through self-correction, through a series of failures. These are learning opportunities.

Every graduate student, every scientist, working scientist in the lab, whether it’s the wet lab, or computational lab, or in the field, knows that a large proportion of experiments are going to fail, and that setup and expectations need to be adjusted.

Maybe the question needs to be modified. Maybe parameters need to be changed. Again, that learning process, that comes out of failure.

But we never talk about it. We never talk about that process, that iteration, that trial and error, (it’s not random. It’s intentional), but it’s there. We never talk about it when we talk about science to the general public.

Sometimes the rhetoric is more reminiscent of religious belief than actually a scientific fact that has been arrived at through that iterative process, stops and starts, and failures, and consolidation of ideas, and changing the hypothesis, etc. etc.

It’s not that the scientists don’t know what they’re doing, that they’re not following the scientific method, they are, but they’re not communicating that to the public.

I think the best example of that was during the pandemic, the COVID pandemic, when the general public, I have a sense the general public got a little bit confused and tired of scientists advising policymakers and then policymakers making decisions that appeared to flip flop.

You know, "now do this, now wear face masks, then maybe don’t wear face mask, maybe isolate, maybe don’t isolate.”

There were changes of recommendation and position. Now, to somebody who understands the scientific process, this is to be expected. We are in a completely new situation.

Nobody who’s alive today, who does research on the pandemic, has ever experienced a pandemic of this scale. So of course we’re learning as we go along.

It’s natural that it’s going to lead to failures, which then can be corrected.

And again, this is so crucial to emphasize it.

We learn from these failures, and the next decision, the next recommendation, is going to be better informed, better underpinned by facts.

And so taking a step back from this example, communicating that scientific process, which is all about failing, learning from failure, moving on, maybe failing again, taking a step back, taking two steps forward, maybe another step back, and and so on.

I think by missing that opportunity, we miss the opportunity to make science and scientific process more trustworthy, to show that it really is worthy of trust. We talk about trust in science a great deal, rightly so.

We are worried about the fact that trust in science is dropping.

Perhaps by embracing failure, we can reverse that trend.

We can be more transparent, more honest, and therefore bring more people along.

It’s an interesting point to consider whether a conference on failure should itself be a success or failure.

I think whatever we discuss here will be important, will be success.

And I will just end with a quote that I came across by complete coincidence in a bit of a trashy novel that I was reading on holidays recently.

I was very surprised. The quote comes from Winston Churchill, and apparently he said: "Success is the ability to go from one failure to another with no loss of enthusiasm.”

And I actually think that summarizes many of the endeavours that you all engage in, whatever you do.

articles.personality_title: Scientists open up about failure to improve research and trust
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Failure is common in science but rarely discussed openly. This silence makes it harder for researchers to learn from mistakes and slows progress.

**What happened**
In April 2026, Imperial College London and the journal Nature held a conference called Failure in Science. Around 150 scientists gathered to talk about why failure happens, how it affects careers, and how institutions treat it. Magdalena Skipper, editor-in-chief of Nature, and Dr. Stephen Webster from Imperial led the event. They also created a podcast series to explore failure’s role in science.

**Impact**
The conference showed that failure is a natural and important part of science. Scientists often face failure in experiments and funding, but these setbacks can motivate new ideas and stronger careers. For example, a study found researchers who just missed funding often did better later than those who received it. The event highlighted that fear of failure can stop scientists from taking risks, which are needed for big discoveries. It also pointed out that other industries, like tech companies, encourage “failing fast” to learn quickly, something science could benefit from.

**What's next step**
The Good Science Project behind the conference will continue exploring failure in science through podcasts and discussions. The hope is that universities and funders will start to see failure as part of creativity and learning, not just a problem. Better communication about failure could also help the public understand how science really works, increasing trust.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Talking openly about failure in science can encourage risk-taking, improve research, and help people trust scientific discoveries more.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques parlent ouvertement de l’échec pour améliorer la recherche et la confiance
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
L’échec est courant en science mais rarement évoqué ouvertement. Ce silence rend plus difficile l’apprentissage des erreurs et ralentit les progrès.

**Ce qui s’est passé**
En avril 2026, l’Imperial College de Londres et la revue Nature ont organisé une conférence intitulée Échec en science. Environ 150 scientifiques se sont réunis pour discuter des raisons des échecs, de leur impact sur les carrières et de la manière dont les institutions les gèrent. Magdalena Skipper, rédactrice en chef de Nature, et le Dr Stephen Webster d’Imperial ont dirigé l’événement. Ils ont aussi créé une série de podcasts pour explorer le rôle de l’échec en science.

**Impact**
La conférence a montré que l’échec est une partie naturelle et importante de la science. Les scientifiques rencontrent souvent des échecs dans leurs expériences ou leurs financements, mais ces revers peuvent motiver de nouvelles idées et renforcer les carrières. Par exemple, une étude a révélé que les chercheurs qui ont manqué de peu un financement ont souvent mieux réussi ensuite que ceux qui l’ont obtenu. L’événement a souligné que la peur de l’échec empêche parfois la prise de risques, pourtant nécessaires aux grandes découvertes. Il a aussi montré que d’autres secteurs, comme les entreprises technologiques, encouragent « l’échec rapide » pour apprendre vite, ce dont la science pourrait s’inspirer.

**Prochaine étape**
Le Good Science Project, à l’origine de la conférence, poursuivra l’exploration de l’échec en science via des podcasts et des discussions. L’espoir est que les universités et les financeurs considèrent l’échec comme une part de la créativité et de l’apprentissage, pas seulement comme un problème. Mieux communiquer sur l’échec pourrait aussi aider le public à mieux comprendre le fonctionnement réel de la science, renforçant ainsi la confiance.

**Une phrase clé**
Parler ouvertement de l’échec en science peut encourager la prise de risques, améliorer la recherche et renforcer la confiance dans les découvertes scientifiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Los científicos hablan abiertamente sobre el fracaso para mejorar la investigación y la confianza
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
El fracaso es común en la ciencia pero rara vez se habla de él abiertamente. Este silencio dificulta aprender de los errores y frena el progreso.

**Qué pasó**
En abril de 2026, el Imperial College de Londres y la revista Nature organizaron una conferencia llamada Fracaso en la Ciencia. Unos 150 científicos se reunieron para hablar sobre por qué ocurre el fracaso, cómo afecta las carreras y cómo las instituciones lo manejan. Magdalena Skipper, editora en jefe de Nature, y el Dr. Stephen Webster de Imperial lideraron el evento. También crearon una serie de podcasts para explorar el papel del fracaso en la ciencia.

**Impacto**
La conferencia mostró que el fracaso es una parte natural e importante de la ciencia. Los científicos a menudo enfrentan fracasos en experimentos o en la obtención de fondos, pero estos tropiezos pueden motivar nuevas ideas y carreras más fuertes. Por ejemplo, un estudio encontró que los investigadores que casi no consiguieron financiamiento a menudo tuvieron mejores resultados que quienes sí lo obtuvieron. El evento destacó que el miedo al fracaso puede impedir que los científicos tomen riesgos, necesarios para grandes descubrimientos. También señaló que otras industrias, como las tecnológicas, fomentan el “fracaso rápido” para aprender rápido, algo de lo que la ciencia podría aprender.

El proyecto Good Science detrás de la conferencia continuará explorando el fracaso en la ciencia mediante podcasts y discusiones. La esperanza es que universidades y financiadores comiencen a ver el fracaso como parte de la creatividad y el aprendizaje, no solo como un problema. Comunicar mejor sobre el fracaso también podría ayudar al público a entender cómo funciona realmente la ciencia, aumentando la confianza.

**Frase clave**
Hablar abiertamente sobre el fracaso en la ciencia puede fomentar la toma de riesgos, mejorar la investigación y aumentar la confianza en los descubrimientos científicos.

articles.title: We asked teens what schools should teach them about work. This is what they said
articles.summary: Teenagers say they want more work experience at school and opportunities to improve their communication skills.
articles.content:
More than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests.

The online survey, by Survation,, external asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education.

Some called for more support with their communications skills and raised concerns about stress management and personal finances.

Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was the government's "mission" to ensure teenagers leave school "confident about their next step and equipped with the skills and experience they need to succeed".

In England, the government wants to guarantee two weeks' of work experience for every young person, external during secondary school.

It's an opportunity not all teenagers are currently given, the survey for the BBC suggests, with more than half of respondents saying they had not done any.

When teenagers were asked in the survey what skills or guidance they would like more of at school, the most common responses were more work experience opportunities (44%) and help managing finances (43%).

Respondents said they also wanted guidance on how to apply for jobs (42%) as well as how to manage stress and mental health (39%) and develop their communication skills (38%).

As part of the Teen Summit project by Radio 5 Live and Bitesize, the BBC followed four students from Newcastle - Param, McKenzie, Jasmine and Javaris - as they tried out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements.

"I'm terrified about the future. I feel very uncertain about it," 15-year-old Jasmine said.

articles.personality_title_es: Los adolescentes del Reino Unido quieren más experiencia laboral y habilidades prácticas en la escuela
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos adolescentes en el Reino Unido se sienten poco preparados para el trabajo y la vida adulta después de la escuela. Quieren que la escuela les enseñe habilidades prácticas que les ayuden a conseguir empleo y manejar situaciones diarias.

**Qué pasó** – Una encuesta a 2,000 jóvenes de 13 a 18 años mostró que más del 40 % desean más oportunidades de experiencia laboral en la escuela. También quieren orientación para solicitar empleos, manejar su dinero, controlar el estrés y mejorar sus habilidades de comunicación. El gobierno del Reino Unido planea ofrecer dos semanas de experiencia laboral a todos los estudiantes de secundaria, pero más de la mitad aún no han tenido ninguna.

**Impacto** – Esta encuesta revela que muchos jóvenes piden una mejor preparación para la vida real, algo que las escuelas están empezando a atender. Aprender a solicitar empleos, manejar dinero y controlar el estrés puede ayudar a los adolescentes a sentirse más seguros sobre su futuro. El plan del gobierno para garantizar experiencia laboral busca dar a todos los estudiantes la oportunidad de probar trabajos reales, mejorando sus habilidades y preparación.

**Próximo paso** – Las escuelas y el gobierno trabajarán para ampliar los programas de experiencia laboral y mejorar la enseñanza de habilidades para la vida, como la gestión del dinero y la comunicación. Proyectos como el Teen Summit ayudan a los estudiantes a explorar diferentes trabajos y compartir sus experiencias, lo que podría motivar a más escuelas a ofrecer oportunidades similares.

**Frase clave** – Los adolescentes del Reino Unido quieren más experiencia laboral práctica y habilidades para la vida en la escuela para estar mejor preparados para el trabajo y la vida adulta.
